title: 🚨 BITCOIN AFTER THE $6.4B OPTIONS EXPIRY: IS $80K NOW THE BIGGEST BATTLE IN CRYPTO?
subTitle:
🚨 BITCOIN AFTER THE $6.4B OPTIONS EXPIRY: IS $80K NOW THE BIGGEST BATTLE IN CRYPTO?

Bitcoin just had one of its biggest tests of August.

After exploding from roughly $62,000 to above $80,000, BTC is now back around the $78,000 area after failing to hold the $80K level. That means the question has changed.

It's no longer:

“Can Bitcoin reach $80K?”

It already did.

The real question is:

Can Bitcoin stay above $80K? 👀

And the answer may depend on what happens next.

🔥 The $6.4B options event is now behind us

Around 81,700 Bitcoin options worth approximately $6.4 billion expired on Deribit on Friday.

Before expiry, the $75,000 and $80,000 strikes were among the most important areas of open interest, while maximum pain was around $68,000. Calls slightly outnumbered puts.

If you're new to crypto, don't let the word options scare you.

An option is basically a contract that gives a trader the right—but not the obligation—to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price.

So when billions of dollars of Bitcoin options expire, traders pay attention because large positions disappear or are replaced, potentially changing hedging activity and short-term liquidity.

But here's the interesting part:

Bitcoin did not collapse after the expiry.

Instead, BTC remains around the high-$70K area.

That matters.

🟢 Beginner view: Bitcoin is still close to $80K

At the time of writing, Bitcoin is trading around $78K, while Ethereum is around $2.45K.

For a new trader, the chart may look confusing.

Bitcoin went:

$62K → $70K → $75K → $80K → back toward $78K

So is the rally over?

Not necessarily.

A pullback after a rapid rally is normal.

What matters is whether buyers return at lower prices or whether sellers continue pushing BTC lower.

That's why experienced traders aren't simply staring at the $80,000 number.

They're watching the reaction around it.

🧠 Why $80K matters so much

Round numbers have psychological importance in financial markets.

$50K.

$60K.

$70K.

$80K.

They're easy for traders to remember, and large orders can cluster around them.

But $80K has another reason to matter.

Bitcoin briefly reached approximately $81,326 before falling back below $80K, showing that sellers were willing to defend the area.

That creates an important battle zone.

Bulls want:

BTC to reclaim $80K and hold it.

Bears want:

BTC to keep getting rejected around $80K and push lower.

And neither side has completely won yet.

📊 The bullish case

There is still a reason for Bitcoin bulls to be interested.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs recently experienced a strong return of investor demand, including an eight-day inflow streak totaling roughly $2.8 billion, according to recent market reporting.

That is important because ETF flows provide a window into institutional demand.

In simple terms:

If large pools of capital continue putting money into Bitcoin ETFs, that can provide additional buying pressure.

It doesn't guarantee higher prices.

But it is certainly more encouraging for bulls than seeing persistent ETF outflows.

Bitcoin also recently gained roughly 28% during August, making this one of its strongest monthly advances in a long time. Reuters reported that the rally was helped by a weaker U.S. dollar and renewed interest in Bitcoin as an alternative asset.

So the bulls have a story.

And it's not a small one.

⚠️ But here's the bearish problem

Bitcoin has already made a very large move.

Going from approximately $62K to above $80K in a short period means traders who bought much lower now have substantial unrealized profits.

And profitable traders eventually face a decision:

Hold or take profit?

That selling can create resistance.

Recent price action is already showing why the $80K–$81K region deserves attention. BTC briefly pushed above $81K before falling back below $80K.

If BTC repeatedly fails to reclaim $80K, traders may start looking toward lower support areas instead.

One recent market analysis places attention around the $77K area, with $75K becoming a more important level if selling pressure increases.

🐋 The advanced-trader angle: watch volatility

Here's where the story gets more interesting.

The options market is not only about whether Bitcoin goes up or down.

It also tells us how much movement traders are pricing into the market.

Recent Deribit-linked data showed Bitcoin's 30-day implied volatility around 37%, with more than $31 billion in BTC options open interest across listed contracts.

For beginners, implied volatility basically means:

How much movement does the options market expect?

Higher volatility = traders are preparing for larger potential moves.

And after Bitcoin's enormous August rally, volatility is something traders shouldn't ignore.

🎯 What could happen next?

I see three scenarios worth watching.

🚀 Scenario 1: BTC reclaims $80K

If Bitcoin gets back above $80K and actually holds the level instead of immediately falling back, confidence could improve.

The next question would then become whether the market can challenge the recent high around $81K+.

A clean breakout could attract momentum traders.

🐻 Scenario 2: Another rejection

Bitcoin could attempt $80K again and fail.

If sellers continue defending the area, BTC could revisit lower support levels.

This wouldn't automatically mean the entire rally is finished.

It could simply mean Bitcoin needs to cool down after its huge move.

🌀 Scenario 3: Bitcoin chops sideways

Honestly, this may be the most frustrating possibility for traders.

BTC could spend days moving between roughly the upper-$70Ks and $80K without choosing a direction.

That would give the market time to digest the huge August rally and allow traders to see whether demand remains strong.

🟣 And don't forget Ethereum

Bitcoin isn't the only chart worth watching.

Ethereum is currently around $2,450, and ETH has also participated in the recent crypto recovery.

If Bitcoin stabilizes while Ethereum and other major cryptocurrencies continue strengthening, traders may start asking whether capital is beginning to rotate beyond BTC.

But if Bitcoin falls sharply, altcoins can suffer even more because they generally carry greater volatility.

That's why BTC remains the market's main thermometer.

🧩 Five levels of traders, one market

This is the part I think gets missed in most crypto posts.

If you're completely new:

Watch $80K and learn why support and resistance matter.

If you're a beginner:

Watch whether BTC can hold above resistance after breaking it.

If you're intermediate:

Watch ETF flows, market structure and Bitcoin's reaction around $80K.

If you're advanced:

Watch derivatives positioning, implied volatility, liquidity and open interest.

If you're experienced:

Don't just ask where Bitcoin goes. Ask why the market is moving, who is providing liquidity, and whether the move has enough spot demand behind it to continue.

Same Bitcoin.

Five completely different ways to read it.

🚨 My biggest takeaway

The $6.4 billion options expiry was huge.

But the expiry itself wasn't the final story.

What happens after the expiry may be more important.

Bitcoin survived the event and remains near $78K.

But it has also shown that $80K–$81K is not an empty room. Sellers are there.

So I wouldn't call $80K either a guaranteed launchpad or a guaranteed supply wall yet.

The market still has to prove it.

👀 The level I'm watching:

$80,000

If BTC can reclaim it and hold it, bulls may have something to celebrate.

If BTC repeatedly gets rejected there, the market may need to test lower support first.

And that's what makes this setup interesting.

Is Bitcoin simply taking a breather before another attempt at $80K+ — or did the market just show us where the real sellers are?

What do you think? 👇

BTC and ETH are both up, but one is reducing positions while the other is increasing—why does the same leg of上涨 leave two completely different risk profiles? The real question isn’t “will it rise or not,” but who is paying the cost for the next round of volatility.

Facts: On Binance USDT-margined perpetual contracts, $BTC is about $78,059.90, +0.52% over 24 hours, with trading volume of roughly $3.63 billion; $ETH is about $2,455.62, +0.64%, with trading volume of roughly $2.58 billion. Both are in TRADING status. In the past ~6 hours, BTC’s nominal open interest value is -0.10%, while ETH is +0.26%; the latest funding rates are about 0.79/0.39 basis points.

The facts are right here: BTC’s OI has dipped slightly, while ETH’s OI has increased slightly. This doesn’t mean direction is already set. The former could be a relief move from short liquidations/covering, while the latter could be a continuation of direction-driven capital rotation—or even adding leverage early. The market is trying to confirm whether price can validate these two kinds of position behavior separately: whether BTC can hold steady after de-leveraging, and whether ETH’s new positions can persist without having to force the move with higher funding rates.

For a bullish case to hold, both coins’ prices need to keep extending upward, BTC’s OI must bottom out and rebound, and ETH’s OI can rise while the funding rate doesn’t get too overheated. For a bearish case to hold, after price weakens, ETH still increases positions and the funding rate rises, while BTC—despite reducing positions—shifts into adding positions without any rebound.

The most common mistake traders make is assuming that when price is rising, all position increases confirm the move; or, when positions are reduced, immediately concluding that the market has turned bearish. At least two of price, volume, open interest, and funding rate should corroborate each other. When the data don’t align, reducing position size or waiting is itself an effective decision. Especially during weekend periods with thinner liquidity, just a few aggressive trades can make short-term structure look very pretty; but waiting for the next wave of trades and positions to answer the question is often more important than chasing the first move.

My view: I’ll first check whether the divergence is converging—especially whether ETH’s new positions can translate into price returns. The position structure reveals risk earlier than a small price uptick does.

Calling the trend correctly doesn’t necessarily mean executing the trade correctly.

BTC和ETH都在涨，但一边降仓、一边增仓：为什么同一段上涨会留下两种完全不同的风险？真正需要问的不是“涨不涨”，而是谁在为下一步波动付成本。

事实：Binance U本位永续中，$BTC约78,059.90美元，24小时+0.52%，成交约36.3亿美元；$ETH约2,455.62美元，+0.64%，成交约25.8亿美元。两者交易状态均为TRADING。最近约6小时，BTC名义未平仓价值-0.10%，ETH+0.26%；最新资金费率约0.79/0.39个基点。

事实摆在这里：BTC的OI小幅回落，ETH的OI小幅增加。它不代表方向已经确定；前者可能是空头回补后的减压，后者可能是方向资金接力，也可能是提前加杠杆。市场正在确认的是价格能否给两种仓位行为分别兑现：BTC能否在去杠杆后站稳，ETH新增仓能否不靠更高费率硬扛。

多头成立，需要两币价格延续、BTC OI止跌回升、ETH OI增加但资金费率不过热。空头成立，需要价格转弱后ETH仍增仓且费率走高，BTC也从减仓变成增仓却没有反弹。

交易者最容易犯的错，是看到上涨就把所有增仓当成确认，或看到减仓就直接判定转空。价格、成交、持仓和费率至少要有两项互相印证。数据不一致时，缩小仓位或等待，本身就是一种有效决策。尤其在周末流动性较薄的时段，几笔主动成交就能把短线结构推得很漂亮；等下一段成交和仓位给出答案，往往比追第一下更重要。

ETH rises 0.7%, while OI increases only 0.3%: What is leverage betting on this time more boldly than BTC?

ETH has risen less than 1%, yet open interest keeps increasing; BTC, on the other hand, slightly reduces exposure. Why does the same market rebound feel “heavier” in ETH’s leverage? A small rise plus added positions isn’t automatically bullish—it could also mean new long positions are stacking risk first.

The facts: On Binance USD-margined perpetuals, $BTC is around $78,059.90, up +0.52% over 24 hours, with about $3.63 billion in trading volume; $ETH is around $2,455.62, up +0.64%, with about $2.58 billion in trading volume. Both instruments are in TRADING status. Over the most recent ~6 hours, BTC’s notional open interest is -0.10%, while ETH’s is +0.26%; the latest funding rates are roughly 0.79/0.39 basis points.

Why might price action not match “bullish-looking” position increases? OI only indicates that funds are entering—it doesn’t tell you the direction or the quality of the positions. If ETH can continue rising, the added positions act like relay momentum. If price stalls, stop-losses and liquidations from newly added longs can flip and amplify volatility. What the market is confirming is whether ETH’s new positions get a price payoff—not whether anyone has opened trades.

For longs to be “right,” ETH needs to keep moving up, OI should increase slowly, and funding should remain restrained—suggesting it’s not a frenzied chase. For shorts to be “right,” ETH must fall while OI still expands and funding rises; that implies contrarian longs are accumulating.

The most common mistake traders make is seeing a rise and assuming all added positions confirm the move—or seeing reduced positions and immediately calling a shift to shorts. At least two of price, volume, open interest, and funding rate need to corroborate each other. When the data don’t align, reducing position size or waiting is, in itself, an effective decision. Especially during weekend periods with thinner liquidity, a few aggressive trades can make short-term structure look excellent; waiting for the next leg of trades and positioning to answer the question is often more important than chasing the first move.

My view: I care most about whether ETH can hold the gains after the increased positions. If there’s no price follow-through, position increases shouldn’t be treated as a reason to go long.

Being right about the trend doesn’t mean being right about the trade.

That kind of headline makes a lot of traders chase the chart without thinking about what happens if the bid slows down. The trap is simple: people see treasury accumulation, assume the move is guaranteed, and end up buying the top or holding through a flush.

When one buyer controls nearly 1 in every 20 ETH out there, the market starts to feel the flow. That can support price while the buying continues, but it also creates a new risk for $ETH and even spillover sentiment in $BTC and $BNB markets: if that accumulation pauses, the market may have to stand on its own a lot sooner than traders expect.

This is why treasury-driven narratives matter. They are not just bullish headlines, they change liquidity, supply perception, and exit timing. If everyone is waiting for the same treasury buyer to keep absorbing coins, the real danger is not missing the entry. It is assuming someone else will always be there to catch the downside.
